land.text: Gorkha and the hill lands Prithvi Narayan Shah had annexed between 1744 and 1768 (Nuwakot, Dolakha, Makwanpur and the Kathmandu Valley rim)

predecessors.note: The Shah kings of Gorkha announced the 'Kingdom of Nepal' on 25 September 1768: the same state under a new name and from a new capital, not a new people. Cliopatria keeps a separate 'Gorkha Kingdom' row to 1787 beside this 'Nepal' row (1775-); see notes.

land.text: the city-states of Kathmandu, Lalitpur and Bhaktapur, taken 1768-1769, 'completing his conquest of the Nepal Valley'

predecessors.note: Cliopatria's 'Kathmandu' row ends in 1761; Lalitpur and Bhaktapur have no row.

capitals.name: Kathmandu (Kantipur)
capitals.note: Unification of Nepal: the lead has Prithvi Narayan Shah 'moved his capital from Gorkha to a city in Kathmandu Valley' in 1768; the valley section has 'he made Kantipur the capital of the expanded country' after Bhaktapur fell in 1769; the table has 'Kathmandu is declared as the capital' (1769). Coordinates from the gazetteer.

correction.text: Gorkha, Nuwakot, Dolakha, Makwanpur (annexed 1762) and the Kathmandu Valley as it stood in September 1768 (Kathmandu and Lalitpur taken in 1768; Bhaktapur held out until the Battle of Bhaktapur on 14 April 1769)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's Nepal row begins in 1775, but the Unification of Nepal page has the Kingdom of Nepal announced on 25 September 1768 and the Kathmandu Valley taken in 1768-1769. The shape is the core named in the found event: Gorkha with Nuwakot, Makwanpur and the Valley (Bagmati and Narayani zones), without the Kirant lands of the east (1772-1774) and Kaski (1771) that the ledger adds. Repair 2026-10-20 (reviewer sa-05-f, not blocking): a 10 km radius round Bhaktapur (one cell, about 250 km2) is left out of the 1768 shape and comes in by the ledger on 14 April 1769 (Unification of Nepal: 'the Battle of Bhaktapur on 14 April 1769 A.D.'); Bhaktapur is not in the gazetteer, so the radius is a coordinate.

correction.text: Gorkha, the Kathmandu Valley, Makwanpur, Kaski and the Sapta Gandaki region (1771) and the Kirant country up to the Tista (1774): the territory the page dates to 1775; without Lamjung and Tanahun, which the Unification table annexes in 1782

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's Nepal 1775 row (57,000 km2, east of 84.6 E) and its Gorkha Kingdom 1775 row (90,300 km2, the west and north) together fill all of modern Nepal (582 cells, 147,200 km2), which the Unification page contradicts: it dates Kaski and the Sapta Gandaki 1771 and the east up to the Tista 1774, but Bheri only 1786, Jumla 1789 and Doti 1790. The corrected shape is the seven zones from Mechi to Gandaki; the ledger adds Bheri (1786) and the far west (1789-1790) inside the span. The Gorkha Kingdom 1775-1787 rows duplicate the same state and belong to the gorkha-kingdom dossier. Repair 2026-10-20: the Unification table has '1782 | Lamjung and Tanahu is annexed', so two 20 km radii round Besisahar and Damauli (10 cells, about 2,500 km2 of the Gandaki zone) are left out of the 1775-1781 shape and come in by the 1782 gain (neither place is in the gazetteer, hence coordinates).

Adjusted from ok (reviewer sa-05-f). Cliopatria's 1788 shape (665 cells, about 168,000 km2) already holds Jumla (Karnali zone, 82 cells), Doti (Seti 50 and Mahakali 24 cells) and Sikkim, which the Unification table dates to 1789 ('Jumla is annexed') and 1790 ('Doti, Kumaun and Srinagar, Garwal, Hindur, Besahr, Chamba ... is annexed'), and which the Kingdom of Sikkim page gives as domination, never annexation. The corrected shape (467 cells, about 118,000 km2) leaves them out; the ledger adds Jumla in 1789 and Doti in 1790, and Sikkim is the hatched occupation of 1776-1816. The 18 cells east of Sikkim (the Chumbi valley and western Bhutan, 88.7-89.3 E) go with it: the Sino-Nepalese War page returns Kerung, Kuti, Longa, Jhunga and Falak in 1789 and gives Nepal no Tibetan land, and they would otherwise stand as an island. The Teesta strip (West Bengal, the 'up to the Tista' annexation of 1774) stays. Unverified, page silent: Dhawalagiri, Rapti and Lumbini stay in from Cliopatria's shape. The Chaubisi Rajya page has the Chaubisi states annexed 'between 1744 and 1816' without years, and the Prithvi Pal Sen page has the king of Palpa dying in April 1806 and 'Palpa was subsumed into the Kingdom of Nepal', so Palpa (Lumbini zone) may be 1806, not 1788; no page gives its extent, so the shape is left as Cliopatria drew it (see notes).

correction.text: Cliopatria's 1788 shape without Jumla (annexed 1789), Doti (1790) and occupied Sikkim (with the country east of it)

keyframe_review.note: 192,200 km2 as drawn; the corrected shape (709 cells, about 179,000 km2) takes Sikkim and the country east of it out (the Kingdom of Sikkim page: 'Nepalese domination (1776-1792)', never annexation). It adds Kumaon (about 21,700 km2, 79.1-80.9 E, 28.8-30.7 N) in 1791, which the Kumaon Kingdom page confirms: 'in 1791 the Kingdom of Nepal invaded Kumaon' (the Unification table says 1790). Doti and Jumla (1790, 1789) come in by the ledger; the 1788 shape is corrected to leave them out until then.

correction.text: Nepal with Kumaon (1791), Jumla (1789), Doti (1790) and the Teesta strip; Sikkim is the hatched occupation, not Nepali territory

the corrected 1791 Nepal shape (Nepal with Kumaon and the Teesta strip, without Sikkim); the Tibetan border country Cliopatria adds is Nepal's hatched occupation of 1791 to October 1792, not Nepali territory

keyframe_review.note: 208,100 km2 for 1792-1793: Cliopatria adds about 16,200 km2 of Tibetan border country (85.8-89.0 E, 28.1-29.0 N) that the Sino-Nepalese War page does not give Nepal. The Treaty of Betrawati of 2 October 1792 left 'Status quo antebellum' and Nepal had returned its 1788 conquests at Kerung in 1789. correction.text: Nepal with Kumaon, and the strip between the Mechi and the Teesta that Nepal renounced in 1816; Sikkim is occupied, not annexed

keyframe_review.note: 179,900 km2: Cliopatria drops Sikkim and the Teesta strip in 1794. The Anglo-Nepalese War page (infobox) has Nepal renouncing in 1816 the land east of the Mechi extending to the Teesta, so the strip east of the Mechi was Nepal's until then; Sikkim is the occupation of 1776-1816 in the ledger (Kingdom of Sikkim page: 'Nepalese domination (1776–1792)', then 'Nepalo-Bhutanese presence (1792-1816)'). The corrected shape adds the Teesta strip (about 2,000 km2) to Cliopatria's.

correction.text: Nepal with Kumaon and the Teesta strip; Garhwal follows in 1804 (ledger)

keyframe_review.note: 180,100 km2, the 1794 shape unchanged: Garhwal enters Cliopatria's shape only in 1805 (25,800 km2, 78.0-80.8 E), but the Garhwal Kingdom page dates the Gorkha occupation 'from 1803 to 1814' and its infobox has Garhwal 'Conquered by the Gorkhas and merged with the Kingdom of Nepal: 1804', and Amar Singh Thapa's page has the army sent 'in 1804 against Garhwal Kingdom'. The ledger gains Garhwal in 1804; the corrected shape is the Cliopatria shape plus the Teesta strip as above.

correction.text: Nepal with Kumaon, Garhwal and the Teesta strip

keyframe_review.note: 207,400 km2: Garhwal inside (Cliopatria's year; the pages say 1804, one year earlier) and the Teesta strip added as above. The Amar Singh Thapa page says the army 'extended Nepal's territory up to the Sutlej river in the west' after the Garhwal campaign without a year; Cliopatria's 1805-1806 steps (6,600 km2 of hill country, 77.4-78.6 E) are the only dating, so the 1806 hill-states gain in the ledger is confidence 1.

227,200 km2 as drawn; the corrected shape (836 cells, about 211,000 km2) is the 1812 shape with the Teesta strip. Cliopatria adds Sikkim and the country east of it (88.1-89.5 E; about 10,400 km2 with the Chumbi valley and western Bhutan) in 1814 only to drop them in 1815, with no ledger event. The Kingdom of Sikkim page has Sikkim allied with British India against Nepal and 'The Nepalese then attacked Sikkim, overrunning most of the region including the Terai' before the British attack of 1814, and its infobox gives the Nepalese presence until 1816; it never says Sikkim was annexed, so Sikkim stays the hatched occupation of the ledger (repair 2026-10-20, reviewer sa-05-f).

Nepal in 1815, after Almora (27 April) and Malaun (15 May): the hills west of the Mahakali lost, but the western Terai and the Mechi-Teesta strip still Nepal's until the Treaty of Sugauli (4 March 1816); holds for 1815 only, nepal_1816 follows

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's 1815 shape (149,100 km2, 1815-1819) is the post-treaty outline without the Mechi-Teesta strip and the loss is 34 per cent of 227,188 km2, matching the Anglo-Nepalese War page ('approximately one-third of its land'). Repair 2026-10-20 (reviewer sa-05-f, not blocking): both the Kali-Rapti Terai and the Mechi-Teesta strip are dated 4 March 1816 in the ledger (the Sugauli page: 'was signed on 4 March 1816'; the Anglo-Nepalese page: 'formally ratified on 4 March 1816'), so the 1815 shape keeps the western Terai (Cliopatria's modern outline) and adds the strip back; the new keyframe nepal_1816 removes both from 1816. The Anglo-Nepalese War page does not say who held the Terai during 1815.

region.text: the city-state of Kathmandu

ledger.note: 1768: Prithvi Narayan Shah takes Kathmandu. 'Shah took the city-state of Kathmandu in 1768.' Kathmandu was the Malla city-state at the heart of the Nepal Valley.

region.text: Lalitpur (Patan), the second city-state of the Nepal Valley

ledger.note: 1768: Lalitpur falls. Lalitpur followed the same year (the page does not give the month).

region.text: Gorkha and the lands annexed since 1744, with the Kathmandu Valley

ledger.note: 25 September 1768: Prithvi Narayan Shah proclaims the Kingdom of Nepal. 'On 25 September 1768, he officially announced the creation of the Kingdom of Nepal' and 'moved his capital from Gorkha to a city in Kathmandu Valley'; the Nepal page's infobox has 'Unification: 25 September 1768'. The page gives the proclamation, not a boundary: the core is Gorkha with its annexations since 1744 and the Valley.

1768: the capital moves from Gorkha to Kathmandu. The lead says Prithvi Narayan Shah 'moved his capital from Gorkha to a city in Kathmandu Valley'; the valley section has him making 'Kantipur the capital of the expanded country' after 1769, and the table has 'Kathmandu is declared as the capital' (1769).

region.text: Bhaktapur, the last of the three city-states of the Nepal Valley

ledger.note: 14 April 1769: the Battle of Bhaktapur. 'In 1769 he took possession of Bhaktapur, completing his conquest of the Nepal Valley'; the page dates the battle 'on 14 April 1769 A.D.' (Repair 2026-10-20: the region is now the one cell left out of the 1768 shape, so the gain is live.)

region.text: Kaski (Pokhara) and the Sapta Gandaki region

ledger.counterpart: Kaski and the Sapta Gandaki principalities
ledger.note: 1771: Kaski and the Sapta Gandaki region annexed. Unification table: 'Kaski and Sapta gandaki region are annexed' (the table names no month; it conflicts with the text on Nuwakot, so it is treated as confidence 2).

region.text: the Kirant country (Rava, Dingla, Chainpur, Vijaypur) and the strip up to the Tista

ledger.note: 1774: the Kirant country to the Tista. Unification table: 'Chainpur, Vijaypur, area up to Tista river annexed' (1774) after 'Rava, Cisankhu, Dingla was annexed' (1773); the Kirant section has Ram Krishna crossing the Dudhkoshi on 29 August 1772. The lead's fullest extent is 'Sikkim-Jalpaiguri in the east'.

region.text: Sikkim

ledger.note: 1776: Nepal invades Sikkim. Kingdom of Sikkim infobox: 'Nepalese Invasion: 1776' and 'Nepalese domination (1776-1792)', then 'Nepalo-Bhutanese presence (1792-1816)'; the body has Sikkim 'under both the Gorkha and the Bhutanese rule for more than 40 years'. Hatched, not annexed, throughout 1776-1816: the page (re-read 2026-10-20) says only 'invaded', 'domination', 'presence' and 'rule' and never that Sikkim was annexed or incorporated into Nepal. Cliopatria draws Sikkim inside Nepal only in 1788-1793 and in 1814; the corrected keyframes of 1788, 1791, 1792 and 1814 leave it out (reviewer sa-05-f).

region.text: Lamjung and Tanahun, two of the Chaubisi principalities

ledger.note: 1782: Lamjung and Tanahun are annexed. The Unification table row is '1782 | 1840 | 1839 BS. Lamjung and Tanahu is annexed'; the text says only 'Tanahun was officially annexed to the burgeoning Gorkha Empire'. The extent (two 20 km radii round Besisahar and Damauli) is my reading of the two districts. Added in the repair 2026-10-20 (reviewer sa-05-f, thin).

region.text: the Bheri country

ledger.note: 1786: Bheri annexed. Unification table: 'Bheri ara is annexed' (the table's wording).

region.text: the Tibetan border country at Kuti and Kerung

ledger.note: 1788: the Gorkha army enters Tibet. 'The Gorkha troops entered Tibet through Kuti' and 'reached as far as Tashilhunpo' under Damodar Pande and Bam Shah; after a battle at Shikarjong they withdrew toward Kuti and Kerung.

region.text: Kerung, Kuti, Longa, Jhunga and Falak, returned

ledger.note: 1789: the Treaty of Kerung. Nepal returned Kerung, Kuti, Longa, Jhunga and Falak and so did not keep them (the page's account); Tibet was to pay Rs. 50,001 a year to Nepal and stopped after the first year, so fighting resumed in 1791.

region.text: Jumla and the Karnali country

ledger.note: 1789: Jumla annexed. Unification table: 'Jumla is annexed'.

region.text: Doti, the far-western hills

ledger.note: 1790: Doti annexed. Unification table: 'Doti, Kumaun and Srinagar, Garwal, Hindur, Besahr, Chamba 12 and 18 Thakurai (currently India) is annexed (1847 BS)'. The table lumps Kumaon and Garhwal here; the Kumaon page dates Kumaon to 1791 and the Garhwal page to 1803-1804, so only Doti is taken from this line.

region.text: Kumaon, the Chand kingdom, from Almora

ledger.note: 1791: Nepal conquers Kumaon. 'Seeing this opportunity, in 1791 the Kingdom of Nepal invaded Kumaon'; the Chand kingdom was annexed 'by the newly unified Kingdom of Nepal in 1791', the Gorkhas capturing Almora after Mahendra Chand fled. The Unification table says 1790.

region.text: the Tibetan border country held in 1791-1792 (Kerung, Kuti, Digarcha)

ledger.note: 1791: Nepal attacks again. Abhiman Singh Basnet was sent to Kerung and Damodar Pande to Kuti; Pande attacked Digarcha and arrested a Lhasa minister (the page's account). Cliopatria's 1792 shape adds a Tibetan border strip of about 16,200 km2, taken here as the area the Gorkha armies held.

region.text: the Tibetan border country, evacuated

ledger.note: 2 October 1792: the Treaty of Betrawati. 'They concluded a friendly treaty at Betrawati on 2 October 1792'; the infobox gives 'Status quo antebellum'. Both states accept Qing suzerainty over Tibet and send tribute to Beijing every five years (Nepal paid in 1792, 1794, 1795, 1823, 1842 and 1865); the Qing army had reached Nuwakot.

region.text: Garhwal, the Panwar kingdom at Srinagar

ledger.note: 1804: Garhwal falls. Garhwal Kingdom infobox: 'Conquered by the Gorkhas and merged with the Kingdom of Nepal: 1804'; Amar Singh Thapa's page has him commanding the army 'in 1804 against Garhwal Kingdom due to the Garhwal's discontinuance of annual payments', extending Nepal 'up to the Sutlej river in the west'. The Garhwal page's body also dates the occupation 'from 1803 to 1814', so the year is one of two.

region.text: the hill states between Garhwal and the Sutlej

ledger.counterpart: Sirmur, Bushahr and the other hill chiefdoms between Garhwal and the Sutlej
ledger.note: 1806: the hill country to the Sutlej. Amar Singh Thapa's page says the army extended Nepal 'up to the Sutlej river in the west' but gives no year and names no state; the Sirmur State page puts the Gorkha occupation of Sirmur 'between 1803 and 1814' (Ratan Prakash 'installed by Gurkhas' 1803-1804) and the Bushahr page's timeline has '1803 - 1815 : Nepalese occupation' (repair 2026-10-20), so the hill states were occupied from 1803 and the 1806 step of 6,600 km2 (77.4-78.6 E) is Cliopatria's year, the latest the pages allow. The Unification table lists 'Hindur, Besahr, Chamba' with the 1790 line without a separate year. No page names the other states of the step (Keonthal, Baghal, Jubbal and the rest); the year stays a bridge.

region.text: the country round Kangra fort, where the Gorkha army besieged Sansar Chand

ledger.note: 1806: the Gorkha invasion of Kangra. The Sansar Chand page: 'The Gorkhas and the recently humbled hill-states allied to invade Kangra in 1806' and 'They managed to defeat Sansar Chand Katoch, the ruler of Kangra, in 1806 with the help of many provincial chiefs'; 'Sansar Chand was defeated and left with no territory beyond the immediate vicinity of the fortress of Kangra'. The Amar Singh Thapa page tells of the Gorkha army before the fort without a year. The zone is Cliopatria's 1807 salient to 32.7 N; the pages give no extent. Year moved from 1807 to 1806 in the repair 2026-10-20 (reviewer sa-05-f, thin).

region.text: the Kangra country, given up

ledger.note: 24 August 1809: the Gorkhas return to the Sutlej. 'Bada Amar returned to Sutlej river as per agreement on 24 August 1809 AD'; the Gorkhas 'were helpless against the superior Westernized Sikh forces'.

region.text: Kumaon, Garhwal and the hill country to the Sutlej, fought over from Nalapani to Almora and Malaun

ledger.note: October 1814: the Anglo-Nepalese War opens in the west. Nalapani fort was besieged 'between 31 October and 30 November 1814' and Lord Hastings 'formally declared war on the Kingdom of Nepal on 1 November 1814' after a May 1814 Nepalese attack on East India Company outposts in Butwal. The zone is the land Nepal lost in 1815.

region.text: Kumaon

ledger.note: 27 April 1815: Almora falls and Kumaon is lost. 'Bam Shah surrendered Almora on 27 April 1815'; 'The result of this British victory was the capitulation of the province of Kumaon and all of its fortresses.' The Kumaon Kingdom page puts the cession in 1816 with the treaty.

region.text: the Far West: Garhwal, Dehra Dun and the hills up to the Sutlej

ledger.note: 15 May 1815: Malaun and the Far West. Kazi Amar Singh Thapa surrendered after Almora fell; 'The Nepalese positions in the Far West lost control to the British on 15 May 1815.' The Garhwal Kingdom page dates the annexation of Pauri Garhwal to the war's end 'on 21 April 1815' and makes Tehri Garhwal a subsidiary princely state.

region.text: Kumaon, Garhwal and the hill country to the Sutlej

ledger.note: 15 May 1815: the western fighting ends with the surrender at Malaun; the war continued on other fronts until the treaty was ratified on 4 March 1816.

region.text: the lowlands between the Kali and the Rapti rivers, the western Terai

ledger.note: 4 March 1816: the Treaty of Sugauli takes the western Terai. Article 5 required Nepal to cede 'the whole of the lowlands between the rivers Kali and Rapti' and 'all the hill territories' west of the Kali; the Sugauli page says the treaty 'was signed on 4 March 1816' (the Anglo-Nepalese War page: 'formally ratified on 4 March 1816') and the infobox gives 2 December 1815 as the draft. The Anglo-Nepalese War page has 'some of them were returned to the kingdom later in 1816' without a month or a name; the Sugauli page names no returned land and no December 1816 treaty (both re-read 2026-10-20). The whole strip therefore stays out until 1860 (confidence 2).

region.text: the strip east of the Mechi up to the Teesta

ledger.note: 4 March 1816: the Mechi becomes the eastern border. 'The Mechi River became the new eastern border and the Mahakali River the western boundary of the kingdom'; the infobox has Nepal renouncing territory east of the Mechi extending to the Teesta.

region.text: Sikkim

ledger.note: 1816: Sikkim is restored. The Kingdom of Sikkim page brings 'East India Company presence (1816-1858)' and 'territorial concessions by Nepal, which ceded Sikkim to British India'; the Anglo-Nepalese War page has 'Nepal lost all Sikkim (including Darjeeling)'; the Treaty of Titalia follows in 1817. Sikkim is not given to Britain as territory but returned under British protection. Sikkim is the hatched occupation without a break from 1776, since the corrected shapes never hold it as Nepali territory.

1846: the Rana prime ministers take power. After a 1846 plot and the Kot massacre, 'Bir Narsingh Kunwar emerged victoriously and founded the Rana dynasty.' The Shah king stays head of state; same state, same colour (rule 2).

region.text: Kuti, Kerung and Dzongka, taken in the campaign of 1855

ledger.note: 3 April 1855: the Nepalese army enters Tibet. The Nepal-Tibet War page: 'He declared war in March 1855'; 'On April 3 general Dhir Shamsher defeated a small Tibetan detachment at Chusan and captured Kuti'; 'Kerong was occupied by Bam Bahadur without opposition'; 'The capture of Dzongka was the last action of the campaign'; in December Dhir Shamsher 'recaptured Kuti which he burned before retreating to Listi'. Hatched, not annexed: the extent is a 70 km circle round the Kuti-Kerung passes within the Tibetan side of the border (my reading, no page gives one). The tibet dossier (ea-06) has no event for 1855-56.

region.text: Kuti, Kerung and Dzongka, taken in the campaign of 1855

ledger.note: 24 March 1856: the Treaty of Thapathali ends the occupation. The Nepal-Tibet War page: 'In 1856 the war ended with the Treaty of Thapathali' and 'Nepalese territorial ambitions were dropped'; the Treaty of Thapathali page dates the signing 24 March 1856 and has Tibet paying Nepal 10,000 rupees a year, but neither page says in so many words that the captured land was handed back, and the Thapathali page has Jung Bahadur demanding 'the return of all Tibetan land captured by Nepal' with the Chinese ambassador replying that Tibet was not obliged to give land. Cliopatria's 1856 shape holds no Tibetan land, so the occupation is closed here (confidence 2, the end is a reading).

region.text: some parts of the western Terai region

ledger.note: 1860: the western Terai returns. The Nepal page: 'In 1860 some parts of the western Terai region were gifted to Nepal by the British as a friendly gesture because of its military help to sustain British control in India during the rebellion (known as Naya Muluk, new country)'; the sentence before has the Ranas assisting the British 'during the Indian Rebellion of 1857'. The Unification table calls it the return of 'part of Terai (Naya Muluk) from British India' and the Sugauli page lists 'land in western Terai restored to Nepal in 1860'.

28 May 2008: the Kingdom becomes a Federal Democratic Republic. The infobox gives 'Federal Republic: 28 May 2008'; the body has the UN told of the name 'Federal Democratic Republic of Nepal' in 2008 and of 'Nepal' in 2020. Same state, same colour.

wars.name: Unification of Nepal
belligerents: Kaski and the Sapta Gandaki principalities
wars.outcome: Gorkha annexes the Kathmandu Valley (1768-1769), Kaski (1771), Lamjung and Tanahun (1782), the east to the Tista (1774), Bheri (1786), Jumla (1789), Doti (1790) and Kumaon (1791).
wars.note: The page's infobox runs the unification '26 September 1744 - 4 March 1816'; the end date is the Sugauli ratification and not explained on the page. The 1744-1767 campaigns (Nuwakot, Makwanpur, Kirtipur) belong to the gorkha-kingdom dossier. This entry starts in 1768, the start of this dossier's life (reviewer sa-05-f: wars must fall inside the life).

wars.name: Sino-Nepalese War

zones.text: Kuti, Kerung and Digarcha on the Tibetan side

wars.outcome: Stalemate: Nepal returned its 1788 conquests in the Treaty of Kerung (1789) and, after the Qing army reached Nuwakot, concluded the Treaty of Betrawati on 2 October 1792 ('Status quo antebellum'); Nepal accepted Qing suzerainty over Tibet and sent tribute every five years.
wars.note: 1788-1789 first phase (Kuti, Shikarjong, Tashilhunpo, Treaty of Kerung at Khiru); 1791-1792 second phase (Kerung and Kuti, Digarcha, the Qing army to Nuwakot and the counterattack at Jitpurfedi on 19 September 1792).

wars.name: Gorkha conquest of Kumaon
wars.outcome: Kumaon annexed; Gorkha rule lasted 24 years ('cruel and oppressive' in a number of texts).
wars.note: No battle is named on the page beyond the capture of Almora after Mahendra Chand fled.

wars.name: Gorkha conquest of Garhwal
wars.outcome: Garhwal annexed; the royal family went into exile and the Gorkhas ruled the region for twelve years.
wars.note: The page dates the occupation 1803-1814 in the body and the conquest 1804 in the infobox.

wars.name: Gorkha siege of Kangra
wars.outcome: The Gorkha army withdrew to the Sutlej by agreement on 24 August 1809, 'helpless against the superior Westernized Sikh forces'.
wars.note: Not a war article of its own. Start year 1806 from the Sansar Chand page ('The Gorkhas and the recently humbled hill-states allied to invade Kangra in 1806'; repair 2026-10-20, it was Cliopatria's 1807); the end and the withdrawal to the Sutlej are the Amar Singh Thapa page's, and the Sansar Chand page has Kangra Fort 'under Maharaja Ranjit Singh in 1809'.

wars.name: Anglo-Nepalese War

zones.text: Kumaon, Garhwal and the hills to the Sutlej
the Terai lowlands between the Kali and the Rapti
the strip east of the Mechi

wars.outcome: British victory: Nepal lost about one third of its land at the Treaty of Sugauli (ratified 4 March 1816): Kumaon, Garhwal and the hills west of the Mahakali, the Kali-Rapti Terai, the Mechi-Teesta strip and Sikkim; it kept its independence and accepted a British Resident.
wars.note: War declared 1 November 1814; Nalapani 31 October to 30 November 1814; Almora 27 April 1815; Malaun 15 May 1815.

wars.name: Nepal-Tibet War

zones.text: Kuti, Kerung and Dzongka, taken in the campaign of 1855

wars.outcome: Nepalese victory on the page's infobox: Tibet agreed in the Treaty of Thapathali (24 March 1856) to pay Nepal 10,000 rupees a year and to admit a Nepalese agency at Lhasa; 'Nepalese territorial ambitions were dropped'.
wars.note: March 1855 to March 1856. Kuti taken 3 April 1855, Kerung occupied without opposition, Dzongka the last action; Kuti recaptured and burned in December 1855. Added in the repair 2026-10-20 (reviewer sa-05-f, thin); the Treaty of Thapathali page gives the date of signing.

certainty.note: Hill and Himalayan frontiers with Tibet, Sikkim, Garhwal and the western hill states are approximate; the Treaty of Betrawati (1792) defined no line.

The Treaty of Sugauli fixed the Mechi in the east and the Mahakali in the west ('The Mechi River became the new eastern border and the Mahakali River the western boundary'); the Tibetan frontier is approximate, and the Terai strips were disputed and returned in parts.
The 1860 boundary treaty 'revised the Sugauli Treaty'; the Tibetan and Chinese frontier is approximate in the pages opened (no survey line is given).

notes: Written by sa-05-f on 2026-10-20 from nine opened Wikipedia pages (the page budget for 19 shapes is 9). (1) START YEAR AND THE GORKHA ROW. Cliopatria starts 'Nepal' in 1775 and keeps a separate 'Gorkha Kingdom' row (1588-1787) beside it; in 1775 the two shapes are halves of one country (Nepal 57,000 km2 east of 84.6 E, Gorkha 90,300 km2 in the west and north; together 147,200 km2, the modern outline). They are one state: the page has the Kingdom of Nepal announced by the Gorkha king on 25 September 1768. This dossier therefore starts in 1768 and lists gorkha-kingdom as its predecessor; the gorkha-kingdom dossier (another batch) should end its life at 1768 and its 1769-1787 rows should be dropped as duplicates (they are also anachronistic: the Gorkha row draws the modern outline back to 1588, before Kathmandu and the west were conquered). (2) CORRECTIONS TO CLIOPATRIA. 1775-1787 is rebuilt from the dated annexations (the seven eastern zones, with Bheri 1786, Jumla 1789, Doti 1790 added by the ledger). The Tibetan border strip in the 1792-1793 shape is not Nepal's. The Mechi-Teesta strip (renounced in 1816) is missing from 1794-1813. The Kangra salient of 1807-1808 is a siege, not a province. The 1815-1859 shapes include the western Terai, which Sugauli took and 1860 returned (the Kali-Rapti lowlands are drawn as a 60 km and 50 km radius round Dhangarhi and Nepalganj, about 10,400 km2, a reading of the page's 'western Terai'). (3) WHAT THE PAGES DO NOT SAY. They do not date the annexation of the Dhawalagiri, Rapti and Lumbini zones (Palpa is mentioned only as a governorship after 1806 on the Amar Singh Thapa page), nor of Tanahun; Cliopatria's 1788 shape includes them and they stay in (unverified; see the repair paragraph). They do not name the hill states taken between Garhwal and the Sutlej (the 1806 gain is confidence 1), the start of the Kangra siege (1807, confidence 1), or which Terai lands came back in 1816. The Sikkim page's two labels (domination to 1792, presence to 1816) are kept as one occupation, 1776-1816, and the page never says Sikkim was annexed; Cliopatria draws Sikkim inside Nepal only in 1788-1793 and in 1814, and the corrected keyframes of those years leave it out. (4) NOT OPENED (page budget): the Nepal-Tibet War of 1855-56 and the Treaty of Thapathali, the Anglo-Nepalese Treaty of 1923, the Sino-Nepal boundary treaty (the modern northern frontier), and any ruler list, so identity.rulers is omitted. A gap-filler should open 'Nepal-Tibet War' and 'Treaty of Thapathali' and 'Tehri Garhwal'. (5) COUNTERPARTS WITHOUT DOSSIERS: kingdom-of-sikkim, garhwal-kingdom, kumaon-kingdom, kangra-state, the Malla city-states of Lalitpur and Bhaktapur, Doti, Jumla and the Kirant chiefdoms; the qing-dynasty dossier should record the Betrawati tribute (vassal-like) from its side. Region names the gazetteer lacks: Kirant/Limbuwan, Kumaon, Garhwal, Terai, Kangra (replaced here by admin1 zones, Cliopatria differences and radii). (6) REPAIR OF 2026-10-20 (reviewer sa-05-f). nepal_1788 is now adjust: Cliopatria's 1788 shape holds Jumla, Doti and Sikkim, dated 1789, 1790 and 1776-1816 occupation by the pages, so they are removed from 1788 and the ledger gains them in 1789 and 1790. Sikkim is removed from the 1788, 1791, 1792 and 1814 shapes (the Chumbi valley and western Bhutan cells east of Sikkim go with it, to avoid an island). nepal_1815 keeps the western Terai and the Teesta strip until the March 1816 treaty and a new keyframe nepal_1816 (1816-1819) takes them out. Bhaktapur is left out of the 1768 shape. New events: Lamjung and Tanahun 1782 (Unification table), the Nepal-Tibet War occupation of 1855-56 (Nepal-Tibet War and Treaty of Thapathali pages); the Kangra contest starts in 1806 (Sansar Chand page); the hill-states gain names Sirmur and Bushahr (their pages date the occupation from 1803). STILL OPEN: no page dates the annexation of Dhawalagiri, Rapti or Lumbini, or of the Uttar Pradesh Terai in Cliopatria's 1788 shape (about 65,000 km2 enters between 1775 and 1788); the Prithvi Pal Sen page has Palpa 'subsumed into the Kingdom of Nepal' after the king's death in April 1806, so Palpa (Lumbini zone) probably entered later than Cliopatria draws it, but no page gives its extent. The terms of the December 1816 return of Terai lands are on no page opened. Pages opened in the repair: 7 more (16 in all against a budget of 9; the extra seven are the reviewer's own 'page to try' list); Bushahr State and Nepalese-Tibetan War did not load under those titles.
